title: How do you avoid a pattern explosion?
summary: Too many small classes from over-applying GoF patterns — the senior fix is consolidation, not more patterns.

slides.markdown:
"How do you avoid a pattern explosion?" usually follows a complaint every engineer has made at some point: "this codebase has too many tiny classes and I can't follow the control flow anymore." The interviewer wants to know if your fix is *more* structure (which usually makes it worse) or genuine consolidation — collapsing accidental complexity back down to match the real complexity of the problem.

The senior signal here is diagnosing *why* the explosion happened before proposing any fix.

slides.sectionTitle: Clarifying question: is the complaint about class count, or about actually losing the control flow?
slides.markdown:
Ask which complaint is actually being made, since the fix differs. "Too many classes" alone might just be an aesthetic preference — some domains genuinely need many small types. "I can't follow the control flow" is the real problem: a request bounces through five one-method classes and no single place shows the whole sequence.

If it's the second complaint, the fix isn't necessarily fewer classes — it might be a coordinating method or comment that makes the sequence traceable again, even if the class count stays the same.

slides.sectionTitle: The answer skeleton: name the cause — a pattern applied per method instead of per real axis of variation — then the consolidation fix
slides.markdown:
Name the cause: a pattern applied **per method** instead of per real axis of variation — someone reaches for a fresh Strategy or Factory every time a method has more than one implementation idea, instead of asking whether these separate patterns are actually managing the same underlying variation.

The fix is consolidation, not more patterns: find the classes that are really just facets of one concept and merge them back into a single, parameterized class or a small set of plain functions. This is the same judgment as [pattern-happy over-engineering](over-engineering-and-pattern-happy-design), applied after the fact instead of before.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: five tiny Strategy/Factory/Decorator classes for what's really one axis of variation
Code: the consolidated version — one parameterized class or a small set of functions replacing the five
Diagram: a class diagram with twelve boxes for three real concepts — the pattern-per-method anti-pattern
slides.markdown:
![Twelve small classes grouped into three circled clusters, labelled: this is really just three concepts wearing twelve classes](assets/pattern-explosion-clusters.svg)

The diagnostic habit worth building: when a class diagram looks like this, count how many *genuinely distinct concepts* it represents versus how many classes exist — a large gap between those two numbers is the pattern-explosion signal itself.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: "how do you tell a real axis of variation from an imagined one before applying a pattern?"
slides.markdown:
Ask whether two implementations of the "same" interface are ever actually swapped for each other in running code, or whether one is always used in production and the other only exists "in case." A real axis has multiple implementations genuinely selected under different real conditions today. An imagined axis has one implementation doing all the real work and a second that exists purely for symmetry or hypothetical future use.

If you can delete every implementation but one and nothing in production breaks, the axis was imagined, not real.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: "does this mean fewer patterns are always better?" — no, name the actual trade-off
slides.markdown:
No — naming the actual trade-off matters more than a blanket rule either way. Too few patterns on a genuinely complex problem produces a tangled, special-cased mess that's just as hard to follow as a class explosion; too many patterns on a simple problem produces the explosion this topic is about.

The correct target isn't a direction ("fewer" or "more") — it's matching structure to the actual number of real, distinct concepts and real axes of variation the problem has, whatever that number happens to be.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: "how do you walk this back in a codebase you didn't design, without a big-bang rewrite?"
slides.markdown:
Treat it as an incremental, [low-risk refactor](refactoring-to-fix-smells), not a rewrite: pick one small cluster of over-split classes at a time (not the whole codebase at once), verify via "find usages" that nothing outside the cluster depends on the individual pieces as separate types, consolidate that one cluster, run tests, ship it as its own small commit, then move to the next cluster.

Doing it cluster-by-cluster, verified and shipped independently, avoids the classic failure mode of a consolidation effort turning into an open-ended rewrite that never lands.

slides.sectionTitle: Weak answer: "just use fewer patterns" with no criterion for which ones to cut
slides.markdown:
**Weak belief:** "The fix for pattern explosion is just to use fewer patterns."

**Why it's weak:** it gives no criterion for *which* patterns to cut, so it either does nothing (nobody knows where to start) or gets applied randomly, potentially removing a pattern that's actually managing real variation while leaving genuinely redundant ones untouched.

**Correct model:** the criterion is real vs imagined axes of variation — consolidate patterns managing imagined variation, keep the ones managing variation that's actually exercised in production.

slides.sectionTitle: Wrong answer: merging unrelated concepts into one "generic" class to cut the count, creating a new coupling problem
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** fixing a pattern explosion by merging several unrelated classes into one "generic" utility or manager class, purely to reduce the total class count.

**Why it's wrong:** if the merged classes represented genuinely distinct concepts that just happened to be over-split, cramming them into one class trades a navigation problem for a coupling problem — now unrelated concerns share one file and one set of dependencies, and a change to one risks breaking the other.

**Correct model:** only merge classes that were genuinely facets of the *same* concept — verify that before merging, don't merge purely to hit a lower class count.

Name the cause: a pattern applied per method instead of per real axis of variation. Distinguish real axes (multiple implementations genuinely swapped in production) from imagined ones (one real implementation, one that exists just in case) before deciding what to consolidate. Walk it back cluster by cluster, verified with "find usages" and shipped as small, independent commits — not a big-bang rewrite.

The target isn't "fewer patterns" or "more patterns" — it's structure matching the problem's actual number of real, distinct concepts, and merging only classes that are genuinely the same concept, not just any classes to hit a lower count.
